item.title: Unions Rally Around the Threat of A.I.
item.description:
Tim Suitter knows change is coming to Bath Iron Works, creeping up the adjacent Kennebec River in Maine like a foreboding fog.

Mr. Suitter, the president of the union that represents more than 4,400 workers who build ships for the U.S. Navy at the shipyard, knows the workers must be prepared for the arrival of artificial intelligence.

“It’s going to be here,” said Mr. Suitter, 50, who has worked at the shipyard for nearly 30 years. “You have to wrap your head around it.”

Last month, when Local S6 of the International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers negotiated a new five-year contract with the defense company that runs the shipyard, the union insisted on updating longstanding language about technology. Now the union must be informed at the “conceptual stage,” rather than at implementation, of “any proposed addition or modified technology, equipment or process,” including A.I. and robotics.

“It was the union trying to force the company’s hand about being more transparent when it comes to A.I.,” Mr. Suitter said. “The sooner we can be part of that conversation and represent the members’ side of it, the better off we are.”

Unions are confronting A.I. as an existential danger to workers, not only because of the possibility of massive job losses but also because of its hand in the widening gap between wages and corporate profits. In April, Liz Shuler, the president of the AFL-CIO, called A.I. “the single biggest threat to working people of our lifetime.”

The threat has galvanized a labor movement that has been on its back foot for years. In terms of public opinion, unions are popular. A.I. is not. And yet union membership is at a low ebb — about 6 percent of American private-sector workers are represented by a union — and unions have been hobbled by state laws and a weakened National Labor Relations Board.

Putting A.I. at the top of the bargaining agenda is part of a strategy to overcome that disadvantage, using negotiations to establish boundaries and, labor leaders hope, direct A.I. from the ground up. As workers and employers try to make sense of the A.I. economy, these contracts could help shape policy.

“There is power, there is leverage right now,” said Moira Bulloch, a spokeswoman for the Communications Workers of America, which represents journalists, flight attendants and call center workers. A.I. policy is being set “contract by contract, employer by employer.”

The machinists union, which represents about 600,000 workers in the United States and Canada in industries like defense, aerospace, railroads and aviation, has been particularly proactive. Recognizing that A.I. portends promises as well as threats, the machinists have crafted model contract language and pushed for early, open conversations with companies that employ their members.

“Unions can set the pace,” said David Sullivan, the general vice president for the union’s eastern territory, who encouraged Local S6 to put in the new language.

About a year and a half ago, Joseph Bonomo, a labor lawyer at Pitta, a law firm in New York, realized that while companies were incessantly talking about A.I. on earnings calls, the unions he represented were not. He set out to change that, starting at the bargaining table.

“A.I. is the hill to die on,” Mr. Bonomo tells union clients. “Because if you don’t have a job at the end of that contract, what good was the contract?”

Mr. Bonomo is working with the machinists’ air transport division as an adviser. Richie Johnsen, who runs the division, said he was fine with A.I. being used as a tool to improve corporate profits that can transfer to his members: “But it shouldn’t be replacing people.”

“We have to put in language into our contracts that addresses that,” he added. “Because that’s the only way that happens.” The machinists represent workers at nearly every U.S. airline. The union is in negotiations with United Airlines and Alaska Airlines, and will begin negotiations with Southwest before the end of the year and with American early next year, Mr. Johnsen said.

When Mr. Bonomo spoke to Mr. Johnsen’s team in June, he began by talking about language. “Define the Function, Not the Marketing Label,” read one of his slides. Corporate speak about A.I. can be euphemistic, vague and mind-numbing.

“Employers may not necessarily say, ‘Hey, there’s a new A.I. system,’” Mr. Bonomo said. “They’re going to label it, characterize it as a scheduling tool, a safety platform, a productivity system, a camera upgrade, some routing software.”

He challenged the machinists to interrogate the jargon. What does the system do? Does it collect data? Make predictions? Is it influencing discipline, staffing, scheduling, pay rates? Did the vendor consult with the union before writing the code?

Unions are particularly concerned that A.I. is going to be used to monitor and discipline workers. Mr. Bonomo urges his clients to press for contract provisions that guarantee human review of reports generated by an algorithm.

“I want to be able to say, at the top: ‘If we come back with a contract for ratification and it doesn’t have this, they’re not going to approve it,’” he said. “‘There’s going be a rat outside tomorrow morning, and there’s going be a line of 1,000 people saying that you’re trying to eliminate jobs.’”

Mr. Bonomo also encouraged the machinists and other unions to leverage A.I. to their advantage. Unions could build their own large language models to harness decades of institutional knowledge and records. They could use A.I. to organize more shops.

“Unions have to be in that driver’s seat,” he said.

Like most Americans, the workers at Bath Iron Works primarily encounter artificial intelligence today in slop on social media, or web searches that spit out paragraphs instead of links. They may regard A.I. with distrust but fail to recognize that it’s already in use all around them.

This disconnect has made Devin Ragnar, who at 33 is one of the younger machinists at the shipyard, particularly nervous. Mr. Ragnar handles communications for Local S6 and has been pushing his colleagues, and the union, to be more aware of the reach of A.I. and more proactive about confronting it.

Last year, Huntington Ingalls Industries, a competitor to the shipyard, announced a partnership with Hyundai Heavy Industry that yielded a pilot program to bring A.I.-guided welding equipment to shipyards in Mississippi and Virginia.

“In construction, you hear a lot of ‘You can’t automate this!’,” Mr. Ragnar said. They think a robot can’t do the work, can’t climb a ship. But, he said “it’s very real — it’s happening.”

Mr. Ragnar served on the bargaining committee for the new contract at Bath Iron Works and pushed his fellow members to include language on A.I. He and Mr. Suitter said the company had seemed surprised by the request, as if they hadn’t put a lot of thought into the matter.

Recently, Bath Iron Works introduced a programmable arm that could weld — a co-bot, or collaborative robot, in modern parlance. “They didn’t exactly follow our contract language,” Mr. Ragnar said. The union filed a grievance, and is now working with the company to resolve it.

“A big part of our response was — imagine if this was a much more drastic, broad-reaching change?

In the past, the company might have just said, “Hey, we bought this $10 million machine,” according to Mr. Sullivan. In the future, the union would have warning. Mr. Ragnar said that since the contract was ratified, the company was coming to union leaders with questions about technology.

In response to questions, the company, General Dynamics Bath Iron Works, said it was “committed to being transparent with all its employees about future A.I. and new technology initiatives.”

Mr. Ragnar said he did everything he could to avoid using A.I. “If we let A.I. do menial tasks for us, we are letting these machines think for us,” he said. If welders surrendered some of their work to a co-bot, their skills would erode.

“It’s one of the best things about being human — creating, thinking, and problem solving,” he said.

Mr. Sullivan is more optimistic about the constructive use of A.I. in shipbuilding. If an A.I.-guided machine can weld a seam in 15 seconds — a fraction of the time it takes a human, without the risk of injuries — it could mean more ships under construction, and, in turn, more jobs, with a healthier work force.

“Maybe the new technology would be great,” Mr. Sullivan said. “It’s the unknown.”

item.title: Billy Bush Joins Fox News a Decade After ‘Access Hollywood’ Tape Scandal
item.description:
Billy Bush, whose television career unraveled a decade ago with the release of the so-called “Access Hollywood” tape, in which Donald J. Trump bantered with him about sexual assault, is joining Fox News as a contributor.

The exchange with Mr. Trump, which was recorded in 2005, emerged in the closing weeks of the 2016 presidential election, which Mr. Trump won despite the political fallout from the clip.

But the consequences for Mr. Bush, now 54, a nephew of former President George H.W. Bush and a cousin of former President George W. Bush, were severe.

The scandal cost him his job as an anchor of the “Today” show on NBC just a few months after he had joined the flagship morning program and prompted Mr. Bush to issue an apology in which he said he was “embarrassed and ashamed” of his actions.

In a statement on Tuesday released through Fox News Media, Mr. Bush said he was excited for the opportunity to share “my perspective on the people, ideas and moments shaping today’s culture … as well as the ones trying to undo it!”

Mr. Bush will make his debut at 8 p.m. Eastern on Tuesday on “Jesse Watters Primetime” and will appear across all Fox platforms, the company said.

While Mr. Bush was making chitchat with Mr. Trump on a tour bus before taping a segment for the celebrity news show “Access Hollywood” in 2005, Mr. Trump made vulgar comments about women to him and bragged about groping them.

“You can do anything,” Mr. Trump said during the three-minute recording, which was captured on the set of “Days of Our Lives,” where Mr. Trump was making a cameo appearance.

Mr. Bush, who was in his first full year as an anchor of “Access Hollywood,” guffawed at Mr. Trump’s remarks in the video, which was first obtained by The Washington Post about a month before the 2016 presidential election.

The video became not only a political bombshell but also a legal one for Mr. Trump, whom more than a dozen women have accused of sexual misconduct over the years before he was president.

In 2023, a federal jury in New York found Mr. Trump liable for sexually abusing and defaming the writer E. Jean Carroll, who said that Mr. Trump assaulted her in a dressing room of the Bergdorf Goodman department store in Manhattan in the mid-1990s.

Mr. Trump was ordered to pay Ms. Carroll nearly $90 million in damages, a judgment that he is trying to fight.

While Mr. Trump initially apologized for the “Access Hollywood” tape, saying that the words in the recording did not reflect him, he later suggested to allies that it may not have been him on the tape after all.

Mr. Bush, weighing in on the scandal in a 2017 essay in The New York Times, said Mr. Trump had engaged in revisionist history.

“Of course he said it,” Mr. Bush wrote. “And we laughed along, without a single doubt that this was hypothetical hot air from America’s highest-rated bloviator.”

Mr. Bush expressed regret over his role in the tape, which he said must have been traumatic for the women who have accused Mr. Trump of sexual misconduct.

“To these women: I will never know the fear you felt or the frustration of being summarily dismissed and called a liar,” he wrote, “but I do know a lot about the anguish of being inexorably linked to Donald Trump.”

After the scandal, Mr. Bush spent five years as a host of “Extra,” the long-running syndicated entertainment news show, and started a podcast, “Hot Mics With Billy Bush.”

item.title: First Nonstop New York-to-Sydney Flights to Take Off in 2028
item.description:
Qantas Airways plans to begin offering the first nonstop commercial flight ever between New York and Sydney, Australia, by mid-2028, the airline said on Tuesday. The trip will take about 18 hours.

The flight will be the second route in Qantas’s Project Sunrise initiative, which will use the world’s longest-range aircraft for direct flights between Australia and the rest of the world. Qantas had previously announced that nonstop service between Sydney and London would begin in October 2027.

Flight time from Sydney to London will be about 22 hours, which will make it the most lengthy commercial passenger service. Currently, Singapore Airlines operates the longest nonstop service, which requires about 19 hours to fly from New York to Singapore.

Flying nonstop will shave about three hours off Qantas’s fastest current travel time between New York and Sydney, and about four hours off between Sydney and London, the carrier said.

Vanessa Hudson, Qantas’s chief executive, said in an interview that there was a growing number of Qantas customers who wanted to fly nonstop on ultra-long-haul routes.

“They don’t want to stop in the midpoint, and they are prepared to pay a premium to do that,” she said, adding that the airline’s existing service between London and Perth, a city on Australia’s western coast, is its best “commercially performing route.”

Qantas flies nonstop from London to Perth, but is temporarily making a stop in Singapore on flights from Perth to London because of the conflict in the Middle East, an airline spokeswoman said.

Project Sunrise will use Airbus A350-1000ULR jets, which have been developed for Qantas. The jets, which have a roughly 5,280-gallon fuel tank, can fly up to 22 hours, Airbus said in a news release. Qantas said it had ordered 12 of the planes, with the first one to be delivered in April. Ms. Hudson said she anticipated that it could take more than two and a half years for the entire fleet to be delivered.

A test aircraft in July completed a nonstop 24-hour flight from Melbourne to Toulouse, France, a world record for the longest distance flown by a commercial airliner. In 2019, Qantas made its first nonstop flight from New York to Sydney, a 19-hour journey in a Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner with 49 passengers and crew, in order to test how ultra-long-haul flying affects the body.

The new Airbus jets will have 238 seats and four cabins: first, business, premium economy, and economy. Premium seating will take up about 40 percent of the plane. Ms. Hudson attributed that decision to rising demand for premium travel and the realities of aircraft weight constraints.

Tickets for the two routes will go on sale next year, Qantas said. Passengers will be able to buy seats for the Sydney-London route starting in February and for the Sydney-New York route in August. Prices are not yet available, but Ms. Hudson said the airline was considering charging a 20 percent premium above current one-stop services.

When Qantas first announced Project Sunrise in 2017, it said it planned to include service from Melbourne as well as Sydney. Ms. Hudson reiterated that Melbourne was still a priority, but is further down the line.

“The Project Sunrise aircraft will absolutely operate out of Melbourne,” she said, adding that the airline will announce new routes “progressively” as the new jets arrive.

item.title: In Court Filing Defending Media Ban, White House Says Access Is a ‘Privilege’
item.description:
White House officials said in a court filing Tuesday that President Trump had determined that CNN, MS NOW and Politico had breached standards of conduct, leading to their expulsion from the White House grounds.

The alleged violations, said the filing, include “trafficking in verifiable falsehoods about national security and other issues, and publishing sensitive or classified information.”

“Access to the White House is a privilege — not a right,” reads the filing, which argues that Mr. Trump’s action against the three news outlets does not violate the First Amendment and aligns with a long history of presidents favoring some journalists over others.

The filing, furthermore, claims that the White House’s denial of access is a preliminary matter and that the outlets have until Friday to contest the decision.

The clash began last Friday, when Mr. Trump announced on Truth Social, the platform that he owns, that he would ban the three outlets, saying they “shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES.” On Saturday morning, journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico were denied access to the White House grounds and had their press passes confiscated.

By Monday morning, the news organizations had sued, arguing that the president’s ban “brazenly discriminates based on editorial viewpoint,” and was an affront to their First Amendment rights. They said that the move had blindsided its targets, depriving the outlets of the warning that any such drastic action required. They “received zero advance notice that the president would ban a news organization from the White House if he dislikes its coverage,” according to the complaint.

U.S. District Judge Timothy J. Kelly, who was nominated in 2017 by Mr. Trump, will hold an emergency hearing on Wednesday to consider the media outlets’ request for a temporary court order undoing the access ban.

The government filing Tuesday night included copies of letters sent earlier in the day to each banned news outlet. In addition to accusing the organizations of failing to meet standards of conduct, the letters identified specific stories that allegedly either spread falsehoods or threatened national security. The letter to CNN, for example, cited a January 2026 story that “disclosed ‘top-secret’ construction details related to the East Wing bunker,” the letter reads.

One of MS NOW’s alleged infractions, according to a White House letter, was a June 2026 story claiming “a source said that President Trump ‘underestimated the willingness of Iran to resume conflict.’” Politico is accused of publishing a “document detailing funding for the White House ballroom containing intricate descriptions of how the Secret Service would invest in security improvements,” according to a White House letter.

The three media outlets did not immediately comment on the White House’s filing.

In their lawsuit, the media outlets argued that the White House hadn’t afforded them due process to contest their expulsion. In its response, the White House claims that it has provided the companies with “sufficient post-deprivation process.”

In 2018, Judge Kelly ruled against Mr. Trump in another media access case. Mr. Trump had expelled CNN reporter Jim Acosta from the White House grounds. But Judge Kelly ordered his credentials restored, saying Mr. Trump hadn’t given Mr. Acosta enough notice to challenge the action.

Mr. Trump wrote on Truth Social last week that in light of Judge Kelly’s ruling in the Acosta case, the government would “almost without question” have to appeal the upcoming ruling.

Other news organizations have responded to the ban with acts of support and solidarity. The consortium of five TV networks that covers the president as the so-called TV pool — ABC News, CBS News, NBC News, Fox News and CNN — suspended its immersive coverage of Mr. Trump, and some news outlets temporarily withheld publication of photos of Mr. Trump’s events.

item.title: Trump’s Diesel Dilemma
item.description:
Andrew here. On Tuesday at the United Nations, President Trump declared that official U.S. government documents would rename “artificial intelligence” as “superintelligence,” while dismissing safety concerns as a hoax and vowing not to slow down development.

The technology will stay in focus at the U.N. on Wednesday as Dario Amodei of Anthropic and Sam Altman of OpenAI are expected to address world leaders, alongside Clément Delangue of Hugging Face. We’ll have a full report on Thursday analyzing the growing divide between the White House’s full-steam-ahead push and the industry’s calls for more guardrails.

The Nasdaq Composite is in record territory again, and the S&P 500 isn’t far behind.

The main catalyst? Falling oil prices. Traders are growing more optimistic that world leaders at the U.N. General Assembly this week can find diplomatic solutions to de-escalate wars in the Middle East and Ukraine. The hope is that fuel flows can be quickly restored, bringing relief to consumers and businesses.

But are investors again getting ahead of themselves? On Tuesday, President Trump hailed “very good” talks with Iran, but he also threatened to “annihilate” the country in his speech before the General Assembly.

The latest:

Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil, traded below $100 a barrel this morning.

Nasdaq futures are flat on Wednesday as the tech-heavy index’s winning streak hit four trading sessions on Tuesday. Artificial intelligence bulls in particular have been cheering lower oil prices.

The yield on the 10-year Treasury note, which has moved in line with oil prices, was trading at 4.96 percent Wednesday morning.

Energy and wars have loomed large this week at the U.N. President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine, who is set to speak on Wednesday, told The Wall Street Journal that he expected Trump to push Kyiv and Moscow to agree to an “energy cease-fire.” Trump has blamed Ukraine’s attacks on Russia’s energy infrastructure for disrupting global fuel supplies, and for sending diesel prices skyward — an argument that analysts say tells only part of the story.

Zelensky and Trump both said on Tuesday that they wanted to see a quick end to the war in Ukraine. Zelensky told reporters he hoped fighting ceases “before winter.” But he also said he had asked Trump for a new “winter package” of military equipment.

Meanwhile, at the gas pump: The average price of diesel in the U.S. is $6.52 on Wednesday, according to AAA, roughly a half-penny below Tuesday’s record. Some Republicans, especially those in tight electoral races, have been pushing the Trump administration to ban U.S. exports of diesel to help bring cost relief to farmers and truckers.

Trump said on Tuesday that he was open to that. “I’ve called for it,” the president told reporters.

That said, the oil industry and some analysts warn that such a ban could backfire and worsen the global energy crisis. It’s also driving a wedge inside the Republican Party.

DoorDash will pay millions to shortchanged workers. The online delivery company agreed to pay $131.5 million in a settlement with New York City after it underpaid or failed to pay 264,000 delivery workers. (It will also accept closer monitoring of its payment methods.) The deal comes as three mayoral administrations have tried to crack down on delivery firms that city officials have long accused of mistreating workers considered independent contractors.

Todd Boehly’s bid to buy Lukoil’s assets reportedly gains powerful allies. America’s international investment arm, the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation, and the brother of the Emirati president are expected to join the billionaire investor’s consortium, The Financial Times reports, citing unnamed sources. The group is trying to supplant a deal with Carlyle, the U.S. private equity group, which agreed to buy most of Lukoil’s international assets in January after the Russian oil company was hit with U.S. sanctions.

Questions arise about trading in some Kalshi markets. An analysis of trading data by The Wall Street Journal showed that over a third of trades in a market focused on the price of the ether cryptocurrency showed a series of rapid trades largely at the same price. Observers on social media suggested that the activity resembled “wash trading,” artificial trading that had no economic value; Kalshi said the activity represented normal activity.

President Trump has repeatedly dismissed concerns about the safety of artificial intelligence as “a hoax” — even when they came from within the industry — and said that critics of the technology were shortsighted.

He repeated that idea at the U.N. General Assembly on Tuesday, and suggested that all A.I. needed was a rebrand.

“Welcome to the new world of superintelligence — S.I.,” Trump said in his roughly 37-minute address, in his effort to rename what most people still call A.I. Trump added that “all of United States documents” would be changed to refer to superintelligence.

In the A.I. sector, “superintelligence” is a specific term of art referring to artificial intelligence that surpasses humans at thinking across a broad range of tasks. Most researchers say current technology isn’t anywhere near that definition.

The bigger point: Trump made clear that he doesn’t think the U.S. should slow down A.I. development, as figures like Dario Amodei of Anthropic, Sam Altman of OpenAI and Elon Musk of SpaceX have called for.

The president said suggestions by executives and other world leaders to impose more oversight of the technology were “a globalist scheme” to control A.I. that he “totally rejects.”

Trump instead emphasized that he believes maintaining American dominance of A.I. is a national security concern:

We’re leading now over China by a lot and everyone else, and we’re going to keep it that way. We’re going to keep it very, very straight and very strong. I’m not going to stifle growth of something that will be bigger than the Industrial Revolution.

What to watch next: what Trump says about A.I. (and other topics) when he meets with China’s top leader, Xi Jinping, in Washington this week.

Also look out for Trump’s reaction to how others respond to his A.I. rebrand. He made the issue a test of his influence on the world stage: “Let’s see if I have any power,” he said on Tuesday. “Maybe I do and maybe I don’t. We’re going to find out pretty soon.”

Also pay attention to what Altman and others tell the U.N. on Wednesday, Sri Muppidi reports. Altman is expected to speak about the importance of international safety standards for the technology, and about the ability for individual countries to enact the standards under their own laws.

Washington and Silicon Valley have been wrestling with concerns about U.S. companies embracing Chinese open-weight models.

Some worry that these cheaper alternatives to cutting-edge products from Anthropic and OpenAI are a competitive threat and pose potential security risks.

But the latest data suggests that enterprise users are embracing open-weight models, if cautiously, Sri Muppidi reports.

Businesses are beginning to experiment with open-weight A.I. Data shows that the use of these models — which are publicly available for anyone to use how they wish — has increased markedly lately.

The share of enterprise spending on open-weight models has reached roughly 30 percent in recent weeks, according to data from OpenRouter, an A.I. model marketplace, up from around 10 percent at the start of the year.

OpenRouter ranks A.I. models that customers use for their apps or products based on how many tokens, the basic unit of A.I. use, are processed on its platform.

Making the switch: StackBlitz, which developed the A.I. website builder Bolt.new, is one company turning to open-weight alternatives.

“Something on the order of 60 to 80 percent of our inference is done through open-source models, like open-weight models,” Eric Simons, StackBlitz’s C.E.O., told DealBook. (Inference refers to the process of running A.I. models to complete tasks.) “I expect that to get pretty close to 100 percent within the next three to six months.”

Open-weight models are good at executing simple tasks. “The lower-complexity workloads can be delivered with open-weight models with maybe 10 percent of the cost of what a higher-end frontier, proprietary model might be,” Patrick Wendell, a founder of Databricks, a big A.I. data analysis company, told DealBook.

Adoption could speed up. Wendell told DealBook that it was only a “matter of time” before enterprise customers, who tend to adopt newer technologies more slowly than start-ups, begin to embrace open-weight models.

Soon after the war in Iran began this year, Formula 1 Grand Prix races in Saudi Arabia and Bahrain were called off.

Now, as the fighting drags on — and there’s renewed conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-backed Houthi militia in Yemen — the fate of two upcoming F1 races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, is looking cloudy.

Whether they go on as planned could provide a hint of what may happen with other major events in the region, Niko Gallogly reports.

The F1 races are scheduled for November (Qatar) and December (Abu Dhabi). Formula One Group, the race’s organizer, is expected to decide whether to hold them by the end of the month.

Other racing circuits have already postponed events, citing “uncertainty in the region” or “the current situation in the Middle East”:

The F.I.A., the global governing body for motor sports, announced last week that it was moving the final round of its World Rally Championship competition to Italy from Saudi Arabia. And the 24H Series recently announced that it was moving a race scheduled in Dubai, United Arab Emirates, to South Africa.

The canceled events in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia contributed to a $407 million drop in second-quarter revenue at Formula One’s parent company, Liberty Media, from the same time last year. (Bahrain’s event was moved to Malaysia.)

The uncertainty hurts Persian Gulf countries’ tourism revenue. Sporting events are part of a regional push by members of the Gulf Cooperation Council — Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates — to expand their event and tourism economy.

Other events have been affected. In March, JPMorgan Chase moved an invitation-only investor gathering to Switzerland from Dubai, and the crypto conference Token2049 was rescheduled for April 2027.

“There’s no baseline forecasting on where to go from here when it comes to the geopolitical situation,” Mohammed Soliman, a senior fellow at the Middle East Institute, a Washington research organization, told DealBook.

For now, planners appear hopeful. Last week, Formula One released its 2027 schedule, which includes a full slate of races in the Gulf.

What to watch: the annual Future Investment Initiative Institute, called “Davos in the Desert.” It’s scheduled to take place in Saudi Arabia at the end of October.

Could regional security risks threaten attendance from the typical A-list group of C.E.O.s?

Deals

Bankers for Paramount are reportedly speaking with investors about a $49 billion debt sale to back its takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery, after a settlement with states that had sued to block the deal. (Bloomberg)

Royal Caribbean agreed to buy a 50 percent stake in Sandals Resorts International in a deal that values the all-inclusive vacation company at more than $6 billion. (FT)

Politics, policy and regulation

“The F.B.I. Anti-Corruption Squad Was Circling Susan Collins — Until Trump Got in the Way” (ProPublica)

San Francisco sued the Trump Media & Technology Group to try to block the company from selling early access to Truth Social posts from the president and other government officials. (NYT)

Best of the rest

Prominent figures in tech, including from Andreessen Horowitz, Anthropic, Nvidia and OpenAI, have founded a two-year “A.I.-native” education alternative to college. (WSJ)

“The kids just aren’t drinking as much”: Farmers in California are abandoning acres of vineyards as demand for wine slumps. (AP)
